\chapter{Something, Somebody, Nobody}
\label{ch:algo-y-nadie}
\hlchaptermodality{317}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can answer with something, somebody, nobody, another and a little in Spanish.}

Complete ES-C317-poco: run algo/nada and alguien/nadie as matched pairs, then add otro and poco with both endings.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[algo]{algo — some, built out of other}

\label{lesson:ES-C317-algo}



\begin{quote}
What was \emph{res nata}? (A thing born.) And what does \emph{todo} do in front of a feminine word? (It becomes \emph{toda}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item nada — the answer when there is none.
  \item todo — a great deal more than this.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{AL-go}, two beats. The \emph{g} is hard, as in \emph{goat}. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{algo} — \textquotedblleft{}something.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{aliquod}: \emph{ali-} plus \emph{quod}. \emph{Quod} is \textquotedblleft{}what.\textquotedblright{} \emph{Ali-} is \textquotedblleft{}other.\textquotedblright{} Together: some other what — a thing not yet specified.

That \emph{ali-} is worth collecting, because English has taken it repeatedly. An \textbf{alias} is an other name. An \textbf{alien} is from another place. To \textbf{alienate} somebody is to make them other. \textbf{Altruism} is caring about the other one.

So Spanish builds \textquotedblleft{}something\textquotedblright{} out of \textquotedblleft{}other.\textquotedblright{} That is not obvious at first, but it is sound. To say \emph{something} is to say: not this particular thing — some other one, unnamed.

\emph{Algo} has one shape and keeps it. It stands for a thing nobody has named yet, and a thing with no name has no gender to agree with.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first of four indefinites.

\emph{Algo} is a thing. The next one is a person, and it is built from exactly the same piece.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{algo}
  \item \emph{sí, algo}
  \item \emph{algo}, then \emph{nada}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{ali-} mean? (Other.) What is an \emph{alias}? (An other name.) And why does \emph{algo} have only one form? (The thing it stands for has no name yet, so no gender.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[alguien]{alguien — the same piece, now a person}

\label{lesson:ES-C317-alguien}



\begin{quote}
What does \emph{ali-} mean? (Other.) And which part of \emph{res nata} survived? (\emph{Nata}, the born part.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item algo — the same word, for things.
  \item la enfermera — one somebody you can already name.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{AL-guien}, two beats. The \emph{gu} is a hard \emph{g}; the \emph{u} is silent and only there to keep it hard. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{alguien} — \textquotedblleft{}somebody.\textquotedblright{}

Take \emph{algo} apart once more: \emph{ali-} \textquotedblleft{}other\textquotedblright{} plus \emph{quod} \textquotedblleft{}what.\textquotedblright{} Now swap the second half. \emph{Quem} is \textquotedblleft{}whom\textquotedblright{} — the person form. \emph{Ali-} plus \emph{quem} is \textbf{aliquem}: some other whom.

\emph{Algo} and \emph{alguien} are the same construction built twice, once for things and once for people. Latin drew that line and Spanish kept it exactly. \emph{Algo} is about a thing. \emph{Alguien} is about a person. They are never swapped.

The spelling holds one trap. \emph{Gu} before \emph{e} or \emph{i} is a hard \emph{g}, and the \emph{u} is doing no work of its own — it is a spacer, put there to stop the \emph{g} going soft. You meet the same spacer in \emph{guitarra} and \emph{guerra}. So this word is \textquotedblleft{}AL-gyen,\textquotedblright{} not \textquotedblleft{}AL-gwyen.\textquotedblright{}

Like \emph{algo}, it does not change. One shape for a man and the same shape for a woman, because the whole point of the word is that you do not yet know which.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The pair is complete.

Two words for \emph{some}: one for what, one for who, both built on \emph{other}. And each of them has an opposite waiting.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{alguien}
  \item \emph{alguien, por favor}
  \item \emph{algo}, then \emph{alguien}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is the \emph{quem} in \emph{aliquem}? (Whom — the person form.) What does the \emph{u} do in \emph{alguien}? (Keeps the \emph{g} hard; it is silent.) And which of the pair is for things? (\emph{Algo}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[nadie]{nadie — nada's twin, and this one is about people}

\label{lesson:ES-C317-nadie}



\begin{quote}
Which of \emph{algo} and \emph{alguien} is for people? (\emph{Alguien}.) And what does \emph{ali-} mean? (Other.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item nada — its twin.
  \item alguien — what this answers.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{NA-die}, two beats. The \emph{ie} at the end is one slide. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{nadie} — \textquotedblleft{}nobody.\textquotedblright{}

Here is the twin that was promised.

\emph{Nada} came from \textbf{res nata}, \textquotedblleft{}a thing born.\textquotedblright{} \emph{Nadie} came from \textbf{homines nati}, \textquotedblleft{}people born.\textquotedblright{} Same participle, same construction, same collapse. Latin said \emph{non homines nati}, \textquotedblleft{}not people born,\textquotedblright{} meaning not a soul. The \emph{non} and the \emph{homines} fell away. What was left was \textbf{nati} — the born ones — meaning nobody.

So Spanish has two words for nothingness and both of them are, underneath, the word \emph{born}. One is singular and neuter, for things. One is plural and human, for people. The negation that made them negative has evaporated out of both.

Put all four together and the shape of the chapter appears. For things: \emph{algo} and \emph{nada}. For people: \emph{alguien} and \emph{nadie}. Some and none, twice over, one line each.

English has \emph{nati} all over it and never once negatively: \textbf{native}, \textbf{natal}, \textbf{nation} (a people \emph{born} in one place), \textbf{nature}, \textbf{innate}. Spanish is the language that took that root and made it mean absence.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four indefinites, in two matched pairs.

\emph{Algo} and \emph{nada} for things. \emph{Alguien} and \emph{nadie} for people. And both of the negatives are the Latin word for \emph{born}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{nadie}
  \item \emph{nada}, then \emph{nadie}
  \item \emph{alguien}, then \emph{nadie}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What was \emph{homines nati}? (People born.) What does \emph{nadie} share with \emph{nada}? (Both are the Latin word for born.) And which one is for people? (\emph{Nadie}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[otro]{otro — the other of exactly two}

\label{lesson:ES-C317-otro}



\begin{quote}
What was \emph{homines nati}? (People born.) And what does the \emph{u} do in \emph{alguien}? (Keeps the \emph{g} hard.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item uno... otro — the pattern this word gets built into.
  \item algo — built on Latin's \emph{other} word for other.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{O-tro}, two beats. The \emph{tr} runs together and the \emph{r} is a single tap. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{otro} — \textquotedblleft{}other,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}another.\textquotedblright{}

Latin had two words where English has one. \textbf{Alius} was \textquotedblleft{}some other, any other, one out of many.\textquotedblright{} \textbf{Alter} was \textquotedblleft{}the other one\textquotedblright{} — of a pair, specifically, when there are exactly two and you mean the one that is not this one.

Spanish kept \emph{alter}. \emph{Otro} is \emph{alter} with the \emph{l} absorbed and the ending trimmed off.

And you have already met the \emph{alius} side of the family. \emph{Algo} and \emph{alguien} are built on \emph{ali-}, which is \emph{alius}. So this one chapter contains both of Latin's words for \emph{other}: one of them turned into \textquotedblleft{}something\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}somebody,\textquotedblright{} the other turned into \textquotedblleft{}another.\textquotedblright{}

English keeps \emph{alter} in the open. To \textbf{alter} something is to make it other. \textbf{Alternate} things take turns at being the other one. An \textbf{alter ego} is your other self. And an \textbf{altercation} is a quarrel — two people, each being the other's problem.

\emph{Otro} changes: \emph{otro} for a masculine thing, \emph{otra} for a feminine one, because it is describing the thing. Same rule as \emph{todo}. An \emph{-o} ending has to agree.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Both of Latin's \emph{others}, inside one chapter.

\emph{Ali-} gave you \emph{algo} and \emph{alguien}. \emph{Alter} gave you \emph{otro}. One word left.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{otro}
  \item \emph{otra vez}
  \item \emph{otro}, then \emph{otra}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What was the difference between \emph{alius} and \emph{alter}? (\emph{Alius} is any other; \emph{alter} is the other of two.) Which one is \emph{otro}? (\emph{Alter}.) And what is an \emph{alter ego}? (An other self.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[poco]{poco — a little, and the circle closes}

\label{lesson:ES-C317-poco}



\begin{quote}
What did \emph{alter} mean? (The other of two.) And what does \emph{nadie} share with \emph{nada}? (The Latin word for born.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item tampoco — this word is already inside it.
  \item mucho — its opposite.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{PO-co}, two beats. The \emph{c} is hard, as in \emph{cat}. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{poco} — \textquotedblleft{}little,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}few.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{paucus}, \textquotedblleft{}few.\textquotedblright{} The \emph{au} flattened to \emph{o} and the ending came off.

You have been carrying it for a long time without opening it. \emph{Tampoco} — \textquotedblleft{}neither, not either\textquotedblright{} — is \emph{tan} plus \emph{poco}: \textquotedblleft{}so little.\textquotedblright{} Every time you have said \emph{tampoco} you have been saying \emph{just as little}, and \emph{poco} is the second half of it.

English has the Latin form in \textbf{paucity}, which means a shortage. It is a formal word and not common, but it is exactly this one.

And English \textbf{few} is the same root arriving down the Germanic road, after the \emph{p} turned to \emph{f}. That is the third time you have seen that shift in these four chapters. \emph{Pie} and \emph{foot}. \emph{Diente} and \emph{tooth}. \emph{Poco} and \emph{few}. Once you can hear a \emph{p} becoming an \emph{f}, a large part of English stops looking foreign.

\emph{Poco} agrees, like \emph{todo} and \emph{otro}: \emph{poco} and \emph{poca}. It is measuring a thing, so it matches the thing.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Twenty words, and the last one closes a circle.

You opened this run with \emph{el pie} and a \emph{p} turning into an \emph{f}. You finish it with \emph{poco} and the same shift. Between the two: the body, what it feels, and the small words that measure both.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{poco}
  \item \emph{poco}, then \emph{poca}
  \item \emph{mucho}, then \emph{poco}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is inside \emph{tampoco}? (\emph{Tan} and \emph{poco} — so little.) Which English word is \emph{paucus} through Latin? (\emph{Paucity}.) And which is it through Germanic? (\emph{Few}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
